title: Why Most Plane Crashes Happen at Takeoff or Landing: Small Plane Crash at Hawkins Field, Jackson
fb_caption: On Saturday, 21 November 2026, a small private plane, a Cirrus SR22, crashed at Hawkins Field in Jackson, Mississippi, about ten minutes after departing a nearby airport. The NTSB is investigating and the cause has not been determined. So why do most plane crashes happen near takeoff or landing, and not at cruise? Height as a safety margin, peak pilot workload, and weather close to the ground, plus why cabin crew ask you to buckle up and listen. Do you listen to the safety briefing? Tell us below.

beats.text: On Saturday, November 21st, a small private plane, a Cirrus SR22, crashed at Hawkins Field in Jackson, Mississippi, about ten minutes after departing a nearby airport. The NTSB is investigating. The cause has not been determined.
It raises a bigger question. Why do most plane crashes happen near takeoff or landing, and not in the middle of the flight?
Takeoff, climb, approach and landing take up only a small slice of a typical flight. Yet industry safety studies consistently find that the majority of accidents happen in exactly those phases.
Here are the three big reasons. One: height is your safety margin. At cruise, pilots can have minutes to sort out a problem. Near the ground, there's very little height, or time, to recover.
Two: workload peaks. In a few busy minutes, the crew changes speed, flaps, landing gear and radio frequencies, while talking to air traffic control.
Three: the ground is close, and so is the weather. Gusty crosswinds and sudden wind shear matter most near the runway, with other traffic and terrain close by.
Think of a tightrope walker. The middle of the rope is the easy part. Stepping on, and stepping off, is where most wobbles happen. Flying works the same way.
That's why cabin crew ask you to keep your seatbelt on, put devices away and listen to the briefing. Many call it the critical eleven minutes: three after takeoff, eight before landing.

So, do you listen to the safety briefing, or tune it out? Tell us in the comments, and send this to someone who flies a lot. Because now you know why the first and last minutes matter most, from Jackson, Mississippi, to every airport in the world.
